tinygo: The host must call the exported `_initialize` before any other export (the WASI reactor convention); Go's `init()` and the runtime start there. True of every probe, so it is not a cost on any one feature.
kotlin: The host must run `_start` (the WASI command convention) before any other export; true of every module that built. Feature 17 (`externref`) is built for the `wasm-js` target, every other probe for `wasm-wasi`.
swift: Every probe is built freestanding in Embedded Swift (`swiftc -target wasm32-unknown-none-wasm`, linked by the toolchain's `wasm-ld`), the lowest-level route in the 6.4.0 toolchain and the only one that yields a module without WASI imports or a runtime. Embedded mode is itself behind `-enable-experimental-feature Embedded` in 6.4.0 (`swift-frontend -print-supported-features` lists `Embedded`, `Extern` and `BuiltinModule` under "experimental"), so every variant carries `experimental-api`; so do the underscored attributes (`@_expose`, `@_cdecl`, `@_extern`) and the Builtin module. No start call is needed by the host.

02.note: Limits, stack size and the exported/imported name are linker arguments in `.cargo/config.toml`.

03.note: A private or `const` array of function pointers is folded by LLVM into a `select`, leaving no table and no `call_indirect`; an exported `static mut` cannot be assumed constant, so the indirect call stays without any barrier (an earlier probe used `black_box` for the same effect).

04.note: `--export-table` / `--import-table` link arguments; the table is `__indirect_function_table` / `env.__indirect_function_table`, sized to the address-taken functions plus one (min 3, max 3 when exported). A private or `const` array of function pointers is folded by LLVM into a `select`, leaving no table and no `call_indirect`; an exported `static mut` cannot be assumed constant, so the indirect call stays without any barrier (an earlier probe used `black_box` for the same effect).

05.note: A `.init_array` constructor produces `__wasm_call_ctors`, which nobody calls unless the host does; no start section. wasm-ld (shared with Zig/TinyGo) has no flag to emit one; an LLVM maintainer states it's "not meant for general use, but rather for toolchains" (LLVM discourse, 2019). rustwasm/team#108 (2018) requested this for Rust and went unaddressed; the repo is now archived (2025). Structural, not Rust-specific.

06.note: The default layout puts data after a 1 MiB stack, at 1048576.

09.note: sqrt/ceil/floor/trunc/round_ties_even are not available in `no_std`; `f64::min/max` do not emit `f64.min/max` (only nightly `f64::minimum/maximum` do).

10.note: A `static` is an address in linear memory, never a Wasm global; the global exists only in `global_asm!`.

11.note: `as` casts; the saturating `f64 as i32` and the sign extensions are emitted with the default target features.

12.note: `write_bytes`/`copy_nonoverlapping` become `memory.fill`/`memory.copy` because bulk-memory is on by default; small constant sizes would become plain stores. `memset`/`memcpy` of a run-time size lower to `memory.fill`/`memory.copy`. Copying bytes that were just filled is folded into a second fill (a valid optimisation), so the probe puts a barrier between the two; that is a property of the probe, not a limit of the language.

13.note: `--shared-memory` (with `+atomics,+bulk-memory`) makes the linker emit a passive segment and copy it from `__wasm_init_memory`; the program cannot request a segment or run `memory.init` itself. The nightly build with `-Zbuild-std` gives the same module.

14.note: A tuple or struct return becomes an out-pointer, so the checker's two-argument call corrupts memory and hangs (`stable-tuple`).

15.note: `core::arch::wasm32`. The intrinsics are explicit requests, but LLVM folds `extract_lane(add(splat, splat))` back into scalar code, so the probe (`memory-roundtrip`) sends the splatted operands through volatile memory and uses the result twice; the plain forms (`attribute`, `flag`) keep only `i32x4.splat`.

17.note: On stable, `global_asm!` on wasm32 is rejected (E0658).

18.note: Function pointers always share the one implicit table; two tables exist only in assembly. The functions must also be exported so `ref.func` is valid.

19.note: `global_asm!` declares a table and uses `table.grow/set/get/size`; `core::arch::wasm32` has no table operations.

20.note: `become` (explicit_tail_calls) plus `+tail-call`. Ordinary calls in tail position are only sometimes turned into `return_call` (`flag` emits it in one direction and still overflows).

21.note: Assembly cannot give a global an initialiser expression, so the sum is computed inside the function. `+extended-const` is a real target-feature flag but, like `gc`, only gates LLVM instruction selection — no `core::arch::wasm32` API or assembly directive exposes writing a global's init-expression from an imported global; LLVM's own MC assembler has no syntax for it. Extended-const is consumed internally for relocations only, same structural gap as Zig.

22.note: `global_asm!` with `call_ref`; without `-C target-feature=+gc` the assembler rejects it (`nightly-asm`).

23.note: rust-lang/rust#150111 (merged) adds `target_feature = "gc"` only as a detection flag for tools like wasm-bindgen; its author states GC features are "not accessible through Rust apart from unstable inline ASM," which has no GC-type declaration syntax. Root cause is LLVM itself: Paulo Matos/Igalia (LLVM discourse, Nov 2023) says WasmGC backend funding "dried out" before completion — the identical structural gap confirmed for Zig/TinyGo in this study.

24.note: Follows directly from 23: no struct/array/i31 GC-type infrastructure exists in LLVM's wasm backend for Rust to build casts, subtyping or packed-field access on top of.

25.note: `memory_size::<1>()` is a compile-time error. With assembly, `memory.copy 1, 0` assembles but the linker produces one memory and the module is invalid (`nightly-asm`).

27.note: Module-level assembly (`global_asm!`, unstable on wasm32) declares the tag with `.tagtype` and writes `try`/`throw`/`catch`. The language route is closed: `catch_unwind` compiles to a tag only with `-Zbuild-std`, `panic=unwind` and `+exception-handling` (on stable a panic traps and no tag exists), but that is panic unwinding, not an exception construct: there is no way to declare a tag or throw a value of your own. The `nightly-unwind` and `stable-catch-unwind` probes are kept as evidence and are not a route.

28.note: Module-level assembly writes the whole function: `try_table (catch_all_ref 0)` capturing the exception, `throw_ref`, and an outer `try_table (catch <tag> 0)` (the same function as Zig's). The language route is closed for the same reason as feature 27: `catch_unwind` / `resume_unwind` compile to `try_table` with `catch_ref` and `throw_ref` (the standardised encoding is already the default; `nightly-unwind-new-eh` is the same module), but only as panic unwinding with std rebuilt, not as an exception construct. The `nightly-unwind` probes are kept as evidence and are not a route.

30.note: `#[cold]` on the rare path, with and without `-C llvm-args=--enable-branch-hint`: no `metadata.code.branch_hint` section is produced. llvm/llvm-project#146230 (open draft, implements the section via a new `-mbranch-hinting` flag) is not yet merged — empirically tested against rustc nightly (LLVM 22.1.0): `-C llvm-args=-mbranch-hinting` is rejected as an unrecognized argument, confirming the flag isn't in Rust's bundled LLVM yet; `--enable-branch-hint` is silently ignored. No Rust-specific tracking issue; gated entirely on the open LLVM PR landing, not structurally closed. Confirmed as of 2026-10-09: llvm/llvm-project#146230 is still open (last updated 2026-10-01), so no LLVM-based toolchain here can emit the section from source. A hand-encoded `.custom_section.metadata.code.branch_hint` can be written with module-level assembly or a section attribute (shown for Zig, `module-asm-section`), but it names a function index and a byte offset that exist only after code generation, so it patches the output instead of marking a branch in the source; it is not counted as a way to express the feature. Not tried in Rust itself.

13.note: `--shared-memory --import-memory -mcpu=...+atomics+bulk_memory`: passive segment, initialised by the linker.

14.note: Module-level assembly writes the two-result function (`.functype divmod (i32, i32) -> (i32, i32)`); no feature flag needed. The language route fails: LLVM's wasm backend supports multi-result codegen (`std.Target.wasm.Feature.multivalue`), but exported/imported functions always lower through the Clang-mirrored C ABI (struct return via out-pointer). zig#16639 (open, stalled since 2023) proposes a `callconv(.Wasm)` using `+multivalue`; not implemented.

15.note: `@Vector`. The same folding as in Rust and C happens to the plain forms; `memory-roundtrip` sends the operands through volatile memory and uses the result twice, and every member is emitted.

16.note: `@Vector` loads, stores and bitwise select map to `v128.load/store/bitselect`; the saturating narrow, written as clamp and truncate, does not become `i8x16.narrow_i16x8_s`, in either of two forms tried (`vector`). Module-level assembly writes all three exports (`module-asm`).

The language route is closed: ziglang/zig#10491 ("Support WebAssembly Reference Types") closed as not-planned — core dev: "I'm afraid there's no such thing yet," gated behind Wasm-specific address spaces never built. flags: ref.func rejected by the bundled assembler
18.note: Module-level assembly declares two `.tabletype` tables and calls through each with `call_indirect <table>`. The C route (`ref.func` + `table.set`) does not build here: Zig 0.16 bundles LLVM 21.1, whose assembler reports "invalid instruction" on `ref.func` even through `zig cc` on a standalone .s file, while wasi-sdk's LLVM 23 accepts the same source (`module-asm`, `module-asm-reftypes`). The working variant takes the function pointers in Zig (`&add1`, an index into the implicit table 0) and copies the funcref with `table.get __indirect_function_table` + `table.set`. Not the cause: the `.tabletype` miscompilation tracked as ziglang/zig#13165, which did not occur.

flags: ref.func rejected by the bundled assembler
19.note: No builtin for table operations. Function-level inline assembly assembles but yields an invalid module (`inline-asm`: the asm statement leaves two values on the stack where the compiler expects one). Module-level assembly declares the table and does `table.grow/set/get/size`; the funcref comes from the implicit table 0 via `table.get`, because Zig 0.16's bundled LLVM 21 assembler rejects `ref.func` (see 18).

20.note: `@call(.always_tail, ...)`. Plain calls get `return_call` in one direction at most (`mcpu-tail-call`) and still overflow.

21.note: Zig defines an `extended_const` target feature, but it's consumed internally by LLVM/the linker for relocations (e.g. PIC data-segment offsets), not exposed as global-initializer syntax. Zig global initializers are always evaluated by the comptime interpreter at compile time, which structurally cannot observe a value (an import) that only exists at instantiation time — independent of whether cell 10 (global import) ever gets fixed.

22.note: Function pointers are indices into the implicit table and are called with `call_indirect`. No `function_references` target feature exists in Zig (`std/Target/wasm.zig`'s Feature enum), and more fundamentally LLVM's wasm backend itself has no `call_ref`/typed-function-reference codegen to expose — an upstream gap, not a Zig-specific omission.

23.note: LLVM's own WasmGC backend effort stalled from lack of funding (Paulo Matos/Igalia, LLVM discourse, Nov 2023: "our funding dried out and we ended up not being able to do it"). Not a Zig gap at all — the LLVM backend Zig relies on has no struct/array GC-type support to surface, full stop.

24.note: Follows directly from 23: the same LLVM-level absence (no GC machine types, no struct/array/i31 lowering) applies identically to casts, subtyping, i31 and packed fields, since none of it exists without the base GC-type infrastructure LLVM's backend doesn't have.

25.note: `@wasmMemorySize(1)` compiles; the module then references a memory that does not exist.

26.note: `llvm-intrinsic` declares `extern fn @"llvm.wasm.relaxed.madd.v4f32"(V, V, V) V` and Zig type-checks the call. It is the LLVM intrinsic's name leaking through `extern`, not a documented Zig API, hence `experimental-api` (a judgement; the author should review). The language construct does not work: `@mulAdd` lowers through the generic `llvm.fma` intrinsic, which llvm-bugs#121311 confirms is not reliably pattern-matched to `f32x4.relaxed_madd` even with `+relaxed-simd` (`mulAdd`).

flags: error unions are ordinary control flow
27.note: Module-level assembly declares the tag with `.tagtype` and writes `try`/`throw`/`catch`; the assembler refuses the instructions without `-mcpu=generic+exception_handling`. The language route is closed: error unions are ordinary control flow (`error-union`), and Zig's error-union model never emits `invoke`/`landingpad` IR. The `.tagtype`/`.globaltype` miscompilation feared from zig#13165 did not occur.

28.note: Module-level assembly writes the whole function: `try_table (catch_all_ref 0)` capturing the exception, `throw_ref`, and an outer `try_table (catch <tag> 0)`. There is no path from ordinary Zig code: LLVM's wasm backend emits `try_table`/`catch_ref`/`throw_ref` only as a lowering target for `invoke`/`landingpad` IR (llvm/llvm-project#124381), which Zig's error-union model never generates. The ABSENT.md that stood here said "Absent (confirmed)" for the language route and had not tried assembly.

flags: hand-encoded section lands after the code section
30.note: `@branchHint(.unlikely)` is accepted and produces no hint section; it only sets LLVM branch-weight metadata, a generic optimizer hint. Confirmed as of 2026-10-09: llvm/llvm-project#146230 is still open (last updated 2026-10-01), so no LLVM-based toolchain here can emit the section from source. A hand-encoded `.custom_section.metadata.code.branch_hint` can be written with module-level assembly or a section attribute (shown for Zig, `module-asm-section`), but it names a function index and a byte offset that exist only after code generation, so it patches the output instead of marking a branch in the source; it is not counted as a way to express the feature. In `module-asm-section` the bytes (function 0, the `br_if` at body offset 8) are accepted by V8, which decodes the section wherever it appears, but wasm-ld places it after the code section while the proposal's Overview.md says it appears "only before the code section", so the checker fails it.

LLVM's own attempt to wire this up (D40559, 2017) was abandoned by its author as unsalvageable — the start function runs before memory/table exports exist, so it structurally cannot call imports. An LLVM wasm-backend maintainer states it is "not meant for general use" (discourse.llvm.org/t/53373). Shared upstream limitation across every LLVM-based toolchain in this study (Rust, TinyGo, Zig).

flags: exports are declared in the build file (moon.pkg.json), not in source
01.note: wasm backend: Imports are declared in source (`fn log(x : Int) = "host" "log"`); exports are a list of function names in the build file. wasm-gc backend: Exports are listed in moon.pkg.json.

02.note: wasm backend: The only language here where limits, the exported name and the imported module and field are all configurable. wasm-gc backend: The wasm-gc output still has a small linear memory whose limits, name and import module/field the build file sets (export and import both probed).

03.note: On the wasm-gc backend: function values are GC closures, no table. The module has no table; indirect calls use `call_ref`.

04.note: No table config in moon.pkg.json on either backend (the full link schema exposes exports/import-memory/memory-limits/shared-memory/export-memory-name/heap-start-address and wasm-gc's string-related options, nothing table-related); inline-wasm only substitutes a function body, not module-level sections, so it can't add a table either. `FuncRef[T]` crosses the FFI boundary as externref, not a table slot.

06.note: `link.wasm.heap-start-address` in moon.pkg.json moves the segment the compiler places its static data in; the `Bytes` literal sits 16 bytes into it (an object header), so 1008 puts "WASM" at 1024. The address is chosen by knowing the compiler's object layout and moving the whole static region, like C's `--global-base`, not by naming the literal's address. wasm-gc has no linear data segments at all (`moonbit-gc/heap-start-address`: no segment), so the route exists on one backend only. Without the option the compiler puts the segment at 10000 (`default`).

07.note: No custom-section option in moon.pkg.json on either backend. moonc's generic custom-section encoder (`dwarfsm_encode_wasm.ml`) exists but is wired only to its own DWARF debug-info emission (the `-g` flag), not to a developer-supplied section name/content.

wasm:default.missing: no rotl/rotr operation; inline Wasm text can write i32.rotl, but its parser rejects i32.rotr

wasm-gc:default.missing: no rotl/rotr operation; inline Wasm text can write i32.rotl, but its parser rejects i32.rotr

08.note: wasm backend: `Int::clz/ctz/popcnt` are intrinsics; there is no rotate, so it is written with shifts. `inline-wasm`: `i32.rotl` parses and is emitted, `i32.rotr` is rejected by the inline Wasm parser.

wasm:default.missing: min/max/copysign have no operation that maps to the instruction; inline Wasm text can write f64.nearest, but its parser rejects f64.min, f64.max and f64.copysign

wasm-gc:default.missing: min/max/copysign have no operation that maps to the instruction; inline Wasm text can write f64.nearest, but its parser rejects f64.min, f64.max and f64.copysign

09.note: wasm backend: `sqrt`, `ceil`, `floor`, `trunc`, `abs` map to opcodes; `min`/`max`/`round`/`copysign` do not (`round` rounds half away from zero). `inline-wasm`: `f64.nearest` parses and is emitted; `f64.min`, `f64.max` and `f64.copysign` are rejected by the inline Wasm parser.

10.note: `Ref[T]` (the only mutable-global construct) is a heap cell on both backends, confirmed by the probe. No FFI/config surface imports a raw Wasm global either (only function and memory imports exist), so neither half of the feature has a path on either backend. moonc's wasm-gc codegen does emit real `global` declarations, but only as internal per-type lazy-init placeholder slots, not anything a developer's `Ref`/`let` maps onto.

11.note: wasm backend: `Double::to_int` is saturating (`trunc_sat`); sign extension is not emitted for the shift idiom. Inline Wasm text writes `i32.extend8_s` and `i32.extend16_s` on both backends (`inline-wasm`).

12.note: `Array::fill` / `blit_to` emit `memory.fill` / `memory.copy` on the wasm backend. On the wasm-gc backend they become `array.fill` / `array.copy` on GC arrays instead, but inline Wasm text writes `memory.fill` / `memory.copy` there too (`inline-wasm`).

13.note: wasm backend: The segment holding a `Bytes` literal is active, also with the `shared-memory` link option (`bytes-literal-shared-memory`); there are no raw addresses to copy to. wasm-gc backend: The `Bytes` literal is held in a passive segment (read with `array.new_data`), but no source construct requests one or runs `memory.init`. Re-checked: no moon.pkg.json option, compiler flag, or stdlib function was found for passive-segment control beyond this internal Bytes-literal use, on either backend.

30.note: `_slowPath(x < 0)` (llvm.expect) produces no `metadata.code.branch_hint` section, with or without `-Xllvm -enable-branch-hint`, an option of this toolchain's LLVM 21 that is accepted but changes nothing. Compare C, Rust and Zig. Confirmed as of 2026-10-09: llvm/llvm-project#146230 is still open (last updated 2026-10-01), so no LLVM-based toolchain here can emit the section from source. A hand-encoded `.custom_section.metadata.code.branch_hint` can be written with module-level assembly or a section attribute (shown for Zig), but it names a function index and a byte offset that exist only after code generation, so it patches the output instead of marking a branch in the source; it is not counted as a way to express the feature. Swift has no assembly route at all.
